fullText:
Denkiworks’ debut lets players pull off tricks and pull pints in a stunning, Japan-inspired setting

A freeloading tanuki, mounting debt, and a town full of possibilities will sound familiar to fans of Animal Crossing. Alas, while you won’t find accountability from Tom Nook, Kyoto-based studio Denkiworks has stepped in to heal your financial trauma with a BMX-filled adventure in which a mammal finally pays the price for their years of bad behaviour. “Even Japanese people ask why it’s a tanuki,” jokes Liam Edwards, a game designer at Denkiworks. “They have such a mythological background to them; they’re almost like dragons in terms of their mythology.”

In Tanuki: Pon’s Summer, you play as an adorable but irresponsible critter named Pon, who’s bled the coffers of the local shrine – his home – dry by buying video games and snack food instead of preparing for its semicentennial matsuri. As a result, the shrine is in total disrepair, and important architecture and cultural artefacts – such as the ema stand and the chōzuya – are left cracked and broken, unbefitting a festival half a century in the making.

With a forceful push from his ancestor, Pon takes a job at the local post office, delivering parcels on a tiny bike for cash to pay for repairs and buy event finery. “A key aspect of this project is that we check everything,” says Edwards. Although the development team included local Japanese people, Edwards and co were keen to ensure that all cultural details were accurate. “Can we create a shrine or a festival about a tanuki?” Edwards notes. “We did extensive research,” he continues, adding: “We have a whole internal encyclopedia of shrines and related items.”

As a tanuki, your responses are limited to emojis – which Edwards sees as a metaphor for his early years in rural Japan, when he was unable to fully communicate with neighbours. “You can understand what people are saying to you, but the ability and depth of response is stunted,” Edwards says. “The flip side is, it doesn’t stop any character in the game from helping you, and I think that’s true of Japan as well,” he adds. “I’ve always found in my time here that no matter how hard things are and how much you’re struggling, when you try to communicate, people still want to help you.”

While you motor through sunflower fields and suburban streets to complete delivery jobs, townsfolk will prod you to engage with their fixations by completing pint-sized activities. “A bit like a mini Yakuza game, you’re going to get involved,” Edwards says. There are all manner of extracurriculars to try out, from sumo to pulling pints in a local izakaya – modelled after the team’s real Kyoto watering hole – baseball and fishing. “It became a funny joke that every time you deliver a package, there’s going to be an activity there,” Edwards says. “Which was a nightmare for us because we basically developed 20 different mini-games inside of one game.”

At the core of Tanuki: Pon’s Summer is the BMXing, with Edwards citing the likes of Tony Hawk’s Pro Skater, SSX and Bomb Rush Cyberfunk as inspiration. Using a mixture of button presses and joystick flicks, you can shred down handrails and pull off a surprising number of tricks, from backflips to bunny hops and beyond. “Pon is the vessel through which everything can exist,” says Edwards. “And because he’s tiny, dumpy and he’s funny, the juxtaposition of him doing BMX tricks is just hilarious.”

To pull off this ambitious style, Edwards sought support from Rollerdrome developer Jacob Mills, who helped ensure the world is primed for trick freestylers with responsive physics and plenty of themed stunt obstacles, such as bamboo half-pipes. And while players won’t need to flex intense finger dexterity to progress through the story, Edwards did want to ensure that making your way from point A to B is as fun as possible. “Even if 90% of people don’t know anything about BMXing and they just want to have fun, for that 10% of people who really like BMXing, you don’t want to let them down.”

title: ‘Fortnite on steroids’: the virtual gaming worlds transformed to train British soldiers
description:
Inside Skyral, part of a consortium that won a £2bn MoD contract to help forces game out complex decisions

fullText:
Inside Skyral, part of a consortium that won a £2bn MoD contract to help forces game out complex decisions

On a sunny July day in Riga, Latvia, a Nato convoy drives down a street lined with kebab shops and a pharmacy. At a downtown intersection, there is the sound of an explosion and the lead tank bursts into flame.

These are real streets in Riga – Lāčplēša iela and the downtown corridor of Tērbatas iela. The kebab shops and the pharmacy are on them. The pedestrians who flee after the tank explodes and huddle at a distance are modelled after the population of Riga: some old, some young, some friendly to Nato, others less so.

But the entire thing is a simulation. It has been built by Skyral, a UK company that is part of a consortium that recently won a £2bn contract from the Ministry of Defence to train the British army.

Modern armies have been training in virtual environments for decades. In 2002, the US army launched a video game called America’s Army, initially run on Windows, a multiplayer shooting scenario that aimed to model combat situations but was criticised as being propaganda for the US military.

A new generation of companies are trying to offer something different: intricate, layered models of systems or places that can capture the second-order consequences of events. Skyral aims to allow militaries to recreate cities and even entire countries. The purpose is less to familiarise a fighter pilot with how to handle an F-16, and more to train soldiers and tacticians on the consequences of a decision.

For example, if a missile strike hits a crowded city street, the population will flee. But if that missile knocks out a power station on a cold winter’s day, the same people are likely to shelter in different areas.

There’s limited research on how much a technology like Skyral’s might improve how soldiers are trained. Broadly, games work: earlier research has suggested that service personnel who have trained on flight simulators perform far better in real-world scenarios. But there are limits to how effectively such scenarios model real-world environments, or how transferable they are to combat. That said, running a simulation is easier and cheaper than organising live combat drills – which is why militaries are spending billions on them. They may not perfectly replicate the real world, but they allow soldiers to train key skills on repeat.

The ideas Skyral is offering have been in development for some time. But the UK will be one of the first militaries to integrate the technology deeply into training its forces. The contract comes amid a wider public debate around how much money the UK is allocating to defence, and if this is sufficient to address changing and growing threats.

How is it different than soldiers playing Call of Duty?

It’s “probably a bit more Fortnite on steroids,” says Naomi Hulme, Skyral’s co-chief executive, who co-founded the company with Jason Kennedy, formerly of the military tech company Raydon. Hulme joined the company after 20 years at BAE Systems, soon after the company was spun from Improbable Worlds Limited, a software company focused on gaming engines and the metaverse.

They began with the virtual worlds that Improbable had developed, Hulme said. “If you swap, like, wizards for soldiers and dragons for tanks, it becomes really sort of defence applicable.” But over time, they built something else: a platform that integrates layers upon layers of information to build, as far as possible, a faithful and usable model of a real city and a real battlefield.

Skyral calls this a “digital twin”. The term originally referred to virtual models of machines, such as cars, that enabled predictive maintenance – for example, by simulating how the brake pads might wear down after five years’ use. But it has widened out recently to refer to new, more ambitious efforts to model reality and allow armies – and humanitarian missions and surgeons – to game out complex decisions.

“It has become a buzzword,” says Wiktor Dotter, the chief executive of Power Size Technologies, a defence and automotive-tech company based in Royal Leamington Spa.

Power Size Technologies is working with the UK military – as well as the US and a few others – on a separate set of simulations. The company builds virtual models of energy systems – everything from the batteries in a tank to the solar panels in a desert camp – and offers these to militaries to help them decide how to electrify their equipment.

These technologies are particularly applicable to the military, he says, where procurement is expensive and decisions are political and take time. It is more challenging to trial a new tank than a new car.

“In defence, you will see quickly that if the development of technology is not connected to usability, so everything’s driven by policy and rules,” he says. “What we try to do is say [to the] MoD: ‘You want to try solar panels in the desert? … You can just do that in simulation. You want to have a crazy idea to have a hybrid battle tank? You can just do it right here in simulation. We have enough data to do that.’”

Skyral’s value proposal is to develop ways to train soldiers on the second-order consequences of battlefield decisions – how combat might affect logistics networks, critical infrastructure, and the behaviour of a human population. To do this, it builds extensive models of real cities, such as Riga.

“In defence, you may well be making decisions without understanding the full consequences,” said Hulme. “What we do in a digital environment is you can test those decisions.”

Meanwhile, a cluster of Nato researchers have been working on digital twins, though often more limited setups, such as models of underwater systems. The difference is in degree. Skyral is offering models that extend far beyond a single system, attempting to incorporate layer upon layer of information: the shape of the electrical grid, and the age and education levels of a real population, for example.

“All of these things that up until now have been done in very siloed sort of modelling – you’re taking all of those models and bringing them all together,” said Hulme. “If you impact one, you see the cascading impact.”

title: Spider-Man's great, more handheld gaming – W31
description: My weeknotes from July 28 to August 3, 2026. Featuring Spide-Man, Star Wars, He-Man, and other nostalgic things I guess.
fullText:
When the events I share on my weeknotes are few and far between, it’s often because I wrote a lot of posts already talking about stuff that was interesting to me during the week, so, yeah it happens sometimes! In any case, this is some of the other stuff that happened between July 28 and August 3, 2026!

📅 In case you missed it, I joined Blaugust for 2026, a month long event where the point is to write and participate as much as you want! Of coures, I’m going for the full 31 posts, though there are plenty of tiers available to choose a challenge that fits you best. As long as it gets you to blog it’s okay!

🕹️ So the Anbernic RG SP is about to come out and it’s exactly the same form factor as the original GBA SP, so better looking than the bulkier RG35XX SP I own, and I want it so badly because it looks so good but I also know I should not get it since I literally have no need for it. In any case, do consider it if you are looking for an alternative handheld, it’s extremely good.

🏠 I was home alone once again! It’s the reason I got to complete a game on my Nintendo Switch—which you’ll see down below—as I played it on the living room and had an awesome full TV screen in the dark experience with it.

🔧 Remember when I said our house flooded because of heavy rain and the plumbing being a mess but that it got fixed? Well… it wasn’t fixed. Thankfully we’ve been at home and able to do damage control successfully.

🎥 Once my parents returned from the trip we actually set-up a super tight movie day where we watched Spider-Man: Brand New Day, but we hadn’t eaten yet so we got super fast chinese food, ate in fifteen minutes, and didn’t even stay for the credits because we had a different appointment. It was a flash but it was fun anyway.

💪 No gym at all this week. Once again, being alone most of the week means I prefer to be at home than to do stuff outside. I am returning for sure this week though. I have to admit I didn’t even use my bicycle on the weekend again. I need to commit before the hobby goes cold, I won’t let that happen.

Super Mario 3D World - Me and friends finally returned to this awesome platformer. This time, we dedicated ourselves to collect more of the missing green stars and stamps in earlier levels instead of continuing with the stories. I just feel like we may as well! Given how good of a platformer this has been, and I don’t really plan on revisiting it once I beat it once, so yeah. Super fun either way!

Fire Emblem Awakening - I beat a couple of side quests to level up characters in my roster, but I made no progress on the main story this week. I did try and failed a couple times, as I lost some characters early on that I wasn’t meaning to. In any case, I am hoping to get better and beat the chapter this week.

Donkey Kong ‘94 - This is also a reason why I slowed down on Awakening. This game is simply super fun! I have been doing world after world and now I’m at the 5th one, with a dozen levels for me to go through. I’m trying to get all the collectibles and most of the RetroAchievements, which makes for a wonderful incentive for me to keep going at it. Wonderful level and puzzle design!

Masters of the Universe - We saw this on Amazon Prime (it’s a shared account I don’t pay for btw) and kind of really enjoyed it! It was a very self-aware movie that really felt like a Saturday Morning Cartoon. I never watched the original He-Man, but I felt it would be a fun time. We ended up laughing quite a bit at how ridiculous it was, worth a watch I’d say.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day - Now. No jokes here. This movie is Tom Holland’s best Spider-Man film, and this is by a very, very long margin. The best Spider-Man film since the Raimi’s Spider-Man 2. The character, the plot, the conflict at hand, everything was handled extremely well. This is also the best looking Marvel movie in ages, it feels like actual film done by people who know the character and truly had a story to tell. Of course, the action does not stay behind at all. The choreography and sequences were truly epic, everything here is top notch. Maybe my favorite film of the year. Even my parents want to watch it again in a couple weeks (because they are busy this weekend). It’s that good.

Leviathan Falls - Chapters 12-31. That’s about 20 chapters since last time I mentioned it! Since Sotolf told me I should read more books other than Manga, I decided I’d follow his advice. The last book from The Expanse has proven to be an absolute rollercoaster, with a lot of points of view from conflicting characters which are incredibly interesting to me. The story has started to collide and I can see the point of no return coming soon, I’m going to finish it this week!

Centuria - Chapters 3-38. Well, this story sure managed to catch my intersting. Since the first couple chapters, that main character has met new allies, fought against a bunch of nightmare-ish creatures of the forest, rebelled against a whole kingdom, defeated a powerful enemy and losing another ally in battle. Quite a wild ride, so I’ll keep reading for another bit. I made the mistake of looking up reviews and having people hating on it and affecting me but, I’ll try to see it with my own critical view.

Uncle from Another World - Chapters 26-27. The chapters of this one are much longer than the other, but actually reading my book also cut away some of my time here. In any case, a fun couple of chapters to entertain myself.

title: SingStar Take That anyone? The strange joy of charity shop video games
description:
Hidden gems can be unearthed, but you have to dig deep into the bargain bins of countless outdated Fifas, Wii Fits without the controllers and partially finished quizshow games
As an eternally optimistic charity shop fan, I hold on to the fantasy that one day I’ll walk into my local Oxfam and find a pristine copy of the Sega Saturn shooter Burning Rangers for £1.50. Or perhaps a box full of old Neo Geo carts for a quid each. Sadly, this is now unlikely. Charity shops have caught on to the fact that old video games – like old vinyl albums – are highly collectible, and so they’re putting the good stuff on eBay.
fullText:
Hidden gems can be unearthed, but you have to dig deep into the bargain bins of countless outdated Fifas, Wii Fits without the controllers and partially finished quizshow games

As an eternally optimistic charity shop fan, I hold on to the fantasy that one day I’ll walk into my local Oxfam and find a pristine copy of the Sega Saturn shooter Burning Rangers for £1.50. Or perhaps a box full of old Neo Geo carts for a quid each. Sadly, this is now unlikely. Charity shops have caught on to the fact that old video games – like old vinyl albums – are highly collectible, and so they’re putting the good stuff on eBay. That’s fine, it’s their job to raise money, not to provide opportunist swine like me with bargains. But what games can you find tucked away in your local branch of Barnardo’s? To find out I visited about 40 charity stores across the country. Here is what I discovered on the shelves … And please do share your own charity shop gaming finds in the comments!

Titles such as Dr Kawashima’s Brain Training and Big Brain Academy sold in their millions on the DS and Wii in the mid-00s, accelerated by smart, celebrity-crammed TV advertising. Naturally, there were reams of imitators – seemingly all of which have ended up on charity shop shelves. The original Brain Training is still challenging and fun – although if you grab a copy, be careful to check any saved game files still left in the cart’s memory. I got a copy for a quid, and when I loaded it up, one of the stored usernames was “Martin’s Sex Bitch” (brain age: 35). Steer well clear of all the TV quiz show games that clogged up the DS library. One charity shop I went into had just a single game: Golden Balls, based on the daytime gameshow presented by Jasper Carrott. Reader: I did not buy it.

This was another ubiquitous category. No matter where I went, charity shops were filled with copies of Dance UK, SingStar and Wii Fit, but all lacked the necessary controllers to make them work. There were Kinect games with no Kinect and PlayStation EyeToy games with no camera. Out of all of them, I’d be tempted most by PlayStation 2 SingStar titles – it’ll only cost about £12 on eBay to buy the microphones and adaptor, then you can pick up the dozens of SingStar instalments for a few pounds (Rock Ballads! Motown! Sing along with Disney!) – hey presto, karaoke heaven. Wii Fit is also OK if you’re happy to pay £10 for a balance board on eBay that hasn’t been pounded to death.

Once again, these proliferated on the family-friendly Wii and DS consoles and as they hold little replay value, they show up in great numbers. Peppa Pig, Pirates of the Caribbean, lots of pet games – one store I found in Brighton had at least five horse sims, including Horse Life and Pippa Funnell. Ubisoft’s range of job sims including Imagine: Fashion Designer and Imagine: Teacher were in abundance, though sadly, I didn’t find a copy of Imagine: Journalist, which would have been useful. One title in this genre that was present in at least 65% of the shops I visited was Carnival Games from 2K Play, a wretched collection of fairground mini-challenges including duck shoot, ring toss and balloon darts. The motion controls are appalling and the player avatars are terrifying, dead-eyed monstrosities. If the backrooms had a games area, this would be playing.

Some games sold so well, they have absolutely no value in the secondhand market. You can always count on finding a number of Call of Duty, Assassin’s Creed or Gears of War instalments as well as many copies of GTA V. Some of these are worth rediscovering. The campaign modes in Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare, Modern Warfare 2 and Infinite Warfare are fun, while Assassin’s Creed Brotherhood, Origins and Odyssey are all worth playing – as is Assassin’s Creed 2. I’d also buy Gears of War 2 and Halo 2 for the campaign modes if you’ve not played them. The Mass Effect and Dragon Age titles are often knocking about and still have a lot of charm.

These are still clogging the shelves of charity shops everywhere, despite (or perhaps because of) the fact that a lot of PC owners no longer have CD-Rom drives, and even if they did, they’re likely to face compatibility issues trying to load ancient copies of, say, The Sims 2 or saucy adult adventure title, Leisure Suit Larry: Box Office Bust (the latter might still be in the Frome branch of the Cats and Dogs charity shop if you’re interested). With digital stores such as Steam and GOG stuffed with retro titles at teeny prices, there’s little reason to buy disc PC games now – unless you stumble across an ancient “big box” copy of Doom, Half-Life or Zak McKracken and the Alien Mindbenders. Which you won’t.

They’re still out there, especially at pop-up charity shops and smaller independent stores. I bagged a copy of the rare Japanese role-playing adventure Koudelka at the Rotary Club shop in Frome for a pound, and feel a little guilty about it. I also recently acquired the light gun titles Time Crisis II (PS2) and Time Crisis: Razing Storm (PS3) for £3 each – and I even have a G-Con 2 and PlayStation Move controller to play them with. Elsewhere, I’ve regularly spotted copies of Dead Rising, Bulletstorm, FEAR and Project Gotham Racing – all great fun. Oh and fellow games contributor Jordan Erica Webber recently found Tiger Electronics’ handheld LCD game Poke Ball at the Cats Protection shop in Leamington Spa. I’d have snapped that up.

But if you do find a copy of Burning Rangers on the Sega Saturn it is completely worthless and terrible and you should just send it straight to me.

title: A Line Held Tight – miners, mechs and mismanagement on a distant planet
description:
Deep underground the player joins a colony of ruthlessly exploited pit workers who could be taking on the bosses. How things play out will depend on you
It is rare for video games to feature industrial action as a key theme, but it does happen. There’s the shady Dockworker’s Union in Disco Elysium and the Orbital Workers Union in space adventure Tacoma; then there is Lynx, the evil union-bashing corp in Hardspace: Shipbreaker. Soon we can add A Line Held Tight, a visual novel that puts workers’ rights – and workers’ lives – at the very centre of the narrative.
In the distant future, a colony of miners digs far beneath the surface of an isolated planet, searching for veins of some exotic ore, protected from the poisonous atmosphere within giant mech suits.
fullText:
Deep underground the player joins a colony of ruthlessly exploited pit workers who could be taking on the bosses. How things play out will depend on you

It is rare for video games to feature industrial action as a key theme, but it does happen. There’s the shady Dockworker’s Union in Disco Elysium and the Orbital Workers Union in space adventure Tacoma; then there is Lynx, the evil union-bashing corp in Hardspace: Shipbreaker. Soon we can add A Line Held Tight, a visual novel that puts workers’ rights – and workers’ lives – at the very centre of the narrative.

In the distant future, a colony of miners digs far beneath the surface of an isolated planet, searching for veins of some exotic ore, protected from the poisonous atmosphere within giant mech suits. But the working conditions are woeful and as a strike looms, an unpopular employee named the Canary must decide whether or not to stand with colleagues and fight against suppression. The player, of course, takes on the role of the Canary, navigating personal as well as political struggles in a world rendered in stark monochrome.

Although there are clear parallels with the miners’ strike in 80s Britain, Humble Grove’s three-person team was inspired by a situation closer to home. “My interest in telling a story about a trade union comes from our own industry’s burgeoning union interest in the face of mass layoffs,” says co-founder Cel Davison. “People who write sci-fi generally speaking fall into one of two camps: those who are interested in writing speculative futures and those who use futuristic settings to tell stories that are reflections of our present. We tend to fall into the latter end of that spectrum.”

Using the highly adaptable narrative game engine Narrat, the game provides a dynamic story guided by player choices. The Canary has a complicated personal connection with the mine, the union and its leaders, which the player has to make sense of. “We’re very interested in the internal workings and conflicts within a collective, how they can make or break a political movement. Our protagonist the Canary starts off as someone quite disinterested in politics, but finds themself in situations where they have to decide what and who they really care about. There’s a lot of variables behind the scenes tracking how the mine’s inhabitants feel about the Canary and the decisions they make.”

Although the game is set in the distant future on an alien planet, elements of it are very grounded in British history. It has a traditional folk soundtrack, recorded by two of Humble Grove, Davison and Beck Michalak, who both play at folk sessions in Yorkshire where mining and union-related songs are common. The game’s visuals resemble charcoal sketches providing a stark, almost Victorian feel. “We first got the idea from some wonderful charcoal drawings at the Wakefield Coal Mining Museum,” says Davison. “Charcoal gives a great coal-like feel, and being a traditional medium gives it a grounded textural feel, but conversely when we worked with it we found it can create some very gauzy, ghostly imagery. This really mirrors the way the Canary processes the world as someone trapped in their own head, especially at the beginning of the game.”

Humble Grove’s debut game No Longer Home was a thoughtful meditation on moving house and leaving a life behind; it looks like A Line Held Tight will take a similarly meditative approach. This time however, the themes are more prescient than Humble Grove may have intended. “I hope it helps people consider how their everyday actions can have political consequences,” says Davison. “If I’m being really honest I hope it convinces more people to join a union.”

title: Halo: Campaign Evolved review – they don’t make ‘em like this any more
description:
PC, Xbox, PlayStation 5; Halo Studios/Xbox Game Studios
Halo’s modernised introduction to all that was great about the 00s’ first-person shooter is also a welcome return trip for those of us who were there at the time
This 25th-anniversary remake of Xbox’s most iconic shooter comes loaded with symbolism. It arrives at a time when Xbox’s whole gaming division (and indeed the games business as a whole) is in turmoil. It’s been made by Halo Studios, an outfit that has arguably never quite recaptured the magic conjured by Halo: Combat Evolved’s original developer Bungie, a studio now owned by rival Sony. It has been polished and prettified using Unreal Engine 5, making it look and feel more modern at the expense of visual uniqueness: Halo now looks similar to hundreds of other games made with those same tools, where Bungie’s 2001 original, made with a bespoke engine, still looks austerely distinctive. I never wanted to become this person, but: perhaps things were  better in the old days?
fullText:
PC, Xbox, PlayStation 5; Halo Studios/Xbox Game Studios
Halo’s modernised introduction to all that was great about the 00s’ first-person shooter is also a welcome return trip for those of us who were there at the time

This 25th-anniversary remake of Xbox’s most iconic shooter comes loaded with symbolism. It arrives at a time when Xbox’s whole gaming division (and indeed the games business as a whole) is in turmoil. It’s been made by Halo Studios, an outfit that has arguably never quite recaptured the magic conjured by Halo: Combat Evolved’s original developer Bungie, a studio now owned by rival Sony. It has been polished and prettified using Unreal Engine 5, making it look and feel more modern at the expense of visual uniqueness: Halo now looks similar to hundreds of other games made with those same tools, where Bungie’s 2001 original, made with a bespoke engine, still looks austerely distinctive. I never wanted to become this person, but: perhaps things were better in the old days?

I had my misgivings after opening level, in which the freshly defrosted supersoldier Master Chief fends off an alien attack on a disintegrating spaceship. Originally this was a masterclass in explosive action: you wake up, you look around (once a clever way to determine whether you needed to invert the controls), and you get right into it, firing gaming’s best pistol at chittering alien grunts who scatter from your bullets. Now it’s wrapped in needlessly expanded cutscenes and explanations. Where Halo Studios has made changes to Combat Evolved’s pacing, it really feels noticeable.

After that, however, I spent much less time thinking about what has been changed, and much more thinking about what hasn’t. Nobody really makes single-player shooters like Halo any more: tense, adaptable, challenging. In 2026, we have multiplayer shooters of every imaginable kind; there is little reason for computer-controlled enemies to be intelligent and unpredictable, because we mostly play against other humans, and they provide infinite variation. What we don’t have in abundance in 2026 is atmospheric single-player shooters like this, or Half-Life, or System Shock 2. Solo campaigns in shooters such as Call of Duty have been reduced to flashy “cinematic” shooting galleries. Halo: Campaign Evolved reminded me what we’ve been missing.

The imposing Elites are still the probably cleverest foes I’ve ever played against, and it’s been 25 years. They bark orders and duck away from my fire, and they know how to flank me, when to rush me and how to adapt to my assaults. Every time you die in this game, you come back to a slightly remixed firefight, making it endlessly replayable; I never minded going back to a checkpoint, because it never feels repetitious. In other shooters you simply memorise enemy numbers and positioning, but here you must constantly adapt your play, especially on higher Heroic or Legendary difficulty. And I’d somehow forgotten about the Hunters. The first time a pair of those spiked brutes appeared I reacted on pure decades-old muscle memory: I turned around and fled.

Unfortunately, we still must contend with the Flood. After several levels of brilliant open-ended fights against intelligent foes under the strange light of a foreign sun, suddenly we are transported into a boring, claustrophobic zombie shooter. I maintain that these mid-game levels are extremely bad: shooting 400 identical parasitic baddies with a shotgun while waiting for a floating robot to open a door has never been my idea of a good time. This will be a controversial opinion, but I was grateful for the new waypoints that told me exactly where to go in the maze of zombie-filled corridors that is the Library. It meant that the worst parts of this game were over sooner.

In co-op Halo becomes somewhat less challenging, atmospheric and tactical and significantly more chaotic. Especially when vehicles are involved, the game transforms completely with the addition of other players, thanks to its flexible, open level design and adaptable foes. I played through much of the game in split-screen with my partner – I maintain that playing Combat Evolved with four players just feels somehow wrong – and was reminded exactly why I spent hundreds of hours rinsing this game with friends as a teenager. Halo remains the best companionable shooting game out there.

Campaign Evolved is a good remake of a brilliant game. There are things that are worse: I miss the original Warthog’s erratic handling and the early-00s sci-fi aesthetic, which is simply irreproducible with modern graphics. For all its prettiness, this remake chugs along at times – especially in split-screen it would occasionally slow to a crawl, and we never had to worry about linking various different online accounts and connecting to servers when we fancied a quick game of Halo in 2001. But the core of this game is impossible to mess up. For millions of younger players, Campaign Evolved is a perfect, modernised introduction to everything that was great about the 00s-style first-person shooter. For those of us who were there at the time, it’s a welcome return trip.

Halo: Campaign Evolved is out now

title: After 40 years, Aliens is still shaping the way video games are made
description:
James Cameron’s high-octane film sequel is a blueprint for modern action space slashers
• Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here
It is difficult to believe that James Cameron’s Aliens was released into cinemas 40 years ago. The seminal space shooter took the original Alien – a tense slasher film with a tiny cast and one monster – and transformed it into an intergalactic war movie crammed with wry one-liners, massive guns and an actual boss battle finale. As a 14-year-old, I stood in line at the Tatton Gatley cinema, unsure if I’d be allowed in – I came out three hours later a changed person, my head filled with esoteric military slang and a deep fear of beeping motion detectors. For days afterwards, I slept with my duvet covering my mouth so that no facehuggers could get me.
fullText:
James Cameron’s high-octane film sequel is a blueprint for modern action space slashers

Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? 
It is difficult to believe that James Cameron’s Aliens was released into cinemas 40 years ago. The seminal space shooter took the original Alien – a tense slasher film with a tiny cast and one monster – and transformed it into an intergalactic war movie crammed with wry one-liners, massive guns and an actual boss battle finale. As a 14-year-old, I stood in line at the Tatton Gatley cinema, unsure if I’d be allowed in – I came out three hours later a changed person, my head filled with esoteric military slang and a deep fear of beeping motion detectors. For days afterwards, I slept with my duvet covering my mouth so that no facehuggers could get me. (I was a highly impressionable teenager.)

It’s little wonder that the film has had such a profound effect on video game design. Take the colonial marines, for example. Although the concept of the space soldier had been around in sci-fi novels since the 1930s, most notably in the works of EE “Doc” Smith and Robert Heinlein (the Starship Troopers), Hicks, Hudson, Vasquez and co, were the perfect 80s rendition, combining the witty banter of contemporary buddy cop flicks with awesome weaponry and hi-tech gadgets. Their influence is easy to spot in Doom, where the nameless marine fights ceaseless waves of hellish monsters using a mix of futuristic rifles and good old shotguns. It’s there too in the Halo series, the Spartan soldiers sporting the same armour and mega weapons, cruising about in very similar highly militarised starships and fighting recognisable hive-mind space beasts. Gears of War, Killzone and Marathon all borrow from the same set of costumes and deadly accessories.

Also important to future game designers was the way in which James Cameron opened up the world of Alien after Ridley Scott’s original locked-room mystery of a movie. He beefed up the Weyland-Yutani Corporation, giving us the stencil for dozens of evil video game mega corps; he brought in an array of weapons from handguns to M41A pulse rifles and the M56 smart guns, introducing the idea of a scaled armoury to discover and master; and he employed a structure based around the repeated rhythm of tense exploration followed by explosive encounters that countless games would follow.

It’s weird, then, how difficult it has proven to directly translate the movie into games. While the original Alien spawned a cult 8bit translation and the brilliant Alien: Isolation, Cameron’s sequel is best known for the disastrously bugged Aliens: Colonial Marines, which led to a lawsuit for deceptive marketing. Elsewhere, third-person co-op blaster Aliens: Fireteam Elite drew mixed reviews but has at least birthed a forthcoming sequel, and the 2D Metroid-style game Aliens: Infestation has plenty of fans. My favourite, though, was one of the two official tie-ins from 1986. Aliens: the Computer Game from Electric Dreams Software was a thrilling proto-FPS, allowing you to control several of the movie’s characters as they stalked through an atmosphere processing plant getting attacked by xenomorphs and facehuggers. I’m not sure it’s ever been bettered.

Watching the movie again this week, it’s impossible not to notice all the little scenic and narrative touches that have since shaped how sci-fi action games function. Even the sentry gun, which was cut from the cinematic release and only turned up in the special edition home release, has become a staple special weapon, present in everything from Call of Duty to Helldivers. I wonder how many of today’s game creators were also stood in cinema lines in the summer of 1986, too young to be there, not quite ready to have their minds blown for ever?

Those of us with an interest in the fibre arts are always delighted to see them crop up in other media. Here, embroidered character art helps Scarlet Deer Inn to stand out in a crowded market. Once players are in, they’ll find the charming medieval village has some horrific secrets. Players guide mother-of-two Elise through danger-filled caverns on a quest to find her children and prevent them from meeting a gruesome end, a goal that gained additional meaning when the husband-and-wife developers had a baby of their own. Armed only with a torch, you must keep it lit or likely repeatedly succumb to the darkness. Jordan Erica Webber

Available on: PC

 Estimated playtime: four hours

In what is likely to become a familiar problem for the games industry, Rockstar’s Grand Theft Auto VI marketing schedule is being infiltrated by AI-generated trailers purporting to show scenes from the forthcoming game. Examples include a surfing video and a woman enjoying champagne on a yacht. As Eurogamer points out, the videos are filling a vacuum left by Rockstar’s somewhat stingy approach to releasing in-game footage. The company does not seem to be impressed.

Rather embarrassingly for console manufacturers seeking to go digital only, network outages are back. On Friday, PlayStation Network went down for several hours, leaving players with no access to their games. And on Monday, it was the turn of Xbox, a major outage making it impossible to sign in to user accounts, launch games or download content. While the PlayStation situation has now been resolved, the Xbox network was still having issues at time of press. All hail our disc-less future!

When Valve announced its new Steam Machine PC, fans were intrigued by a custom front plate the company had attached to the machine, which appeared to be an e-ink screen displaying performance data from inside the computer, such as memory and CPU performance. Now, Valve has released all the files and details for what it calls The Inkterface, so owners can build one – and gaming site Aftermath has done just that. Very nerdy, but very cool.

And if you enjoyed reminiscing about Aliens, you might want to check out forthcoming book Aliens: The Video Games by Mike Diver, a complete history of adaptations, including lots of developer interviews.

This week’s question is from Ben via email:

“I want to learn more about the history of video games and I wondered if there are any canonical lists of the best titles – perhaps a gaming equivalent of the BFI’s 250 Greatest Films of All Time or the American Film Institute’s 100 Years 100 Movies?”

Many publications that write about video games have their own top 100 list, although these tends to be compiled by their own critics or readers rather than a broader spread of experts. GQ, GameRant and Rolling Stone all have versions, while IGN has a “mathematically derived” list of the top 500, and we’ve done the best games of the 21st century (so far). For more formal attempts at developing a canon, the Strong Museum has a World Video Game Hall of Fame, MoMA has a games collection (but for some reason its website does NOT want you to find a definitive list!), and for its Art of Games exhibition in 2012, the Smithsonian compiled a list of 80 important titles with the help of gamers and game makers. There have also been a few books on the subject: try Penguin’s 1001 Video Games You Must Play Before You Die (full disclosure: I wrote some of this book), BFI’s 100 Video Games, or Game On!: From Pong to Oblivion – The Greatest Video Games of All Time, compiled by ex-Edge magazine writers.

If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter – email us at pushingbuttons@theguardian.com.

title: Xbox's new bet on advertising could shake up gaming — if players don't revolt
description: Xbox is testing a way for users to stream the games for free by watching ads. Ad execs say the move hints at a bigger advertising play.

title: Microsoft and Amazon Are Both Introducing New Cloud Gaming Options
description: Microsoft's is testing ad-supported Xbox cloud gaming, while Amazon Luna brings free streaming games to Fire TV.
fullText:
Two tech giants, Microsoft and Amazon, took steps last week to move gaming further into the cloud, with each company aiming at a different part of the (gigantic) gaming demographic.

Microsoft is testing a free (albeit ad-supported) cloud-gaming model for Xbox games. Starting today, gamers who signed up for Microsoft's Xbox Insider Program will be able to play games from their library that are cloud-compatible, without paying for a Game Pass Ultimate subscription. They will, however, have to watch ads at the beginning of the session. Microsoft is currently capping playtime at one hour per session; use up your time and you'll have to watch more ads. There's no word yet on how long the test will be running.

Meanwhile, Amazon announced it is going to embed its Luna cloud gaming service directly into Prime Video—but only if you have a Fire TV device. Fire TV users will see a dedicated "Games" tab next to "Movies," "TV shows" and "Sports." They will be able to play titles like Hogwarts Legacy, EA Sports FC 26 and Clue for the cost of their Prime membership.

The two companies clearly have different targets in mind. Microsoft is catering to the kind of "core" gamers who already own a library of titles but might want to play them on secondary devices like phones and laptops. Amazon is going after more casual gamers, and is trying to put their gaming offerings in front of as many eyeballs as possible. It plans to package its games on the same pages as the movie entries for well-known IP like Harry Potter, so someone might decide to play a little game with their remote before they watch a movie.

If you have an Xbox, here's how to check out some ad-supported cloud gaming.

Download the Xbox Insider Hub app on Xbox Series X|S, Xbox One, or Windows PC.

Enroll in the Xbox Insider Program. It's free.

That's it! Now you can stream select cloud-compatible games you own (after you check out some commercials, of course.)

If you have Prime, you can already try Luna. The company isn't adding any extra content for Fire TV users; it's just changing the way it presents the games it offers. Here's how to check it out.

First, you'll need a n Amazon Fire device. That means Fire TV stick, Fire TV Cube, or a smart TV running the Fire TV operating system.

On the main menu, you should see the new "Games" tab.

Click it and go to town. Pro tip: Play Indiana Jones and the Great Circle because it is fantastic.

You can play Luna games with any Bluetooth controller or use your phone as the controller.

title: Glitched into empty space: why video games are obsessed with the Backrooms
description:
The horror movie sensation of 2026 has its roots in gaming’s discovery of ‘noclip’ – and the hidden virtual realms that could be opened up inside games. Developers explain how everyone got lost in these liminal spaces
It starts on 4chan, in a May 2019 thread entitled “unsettling images”. The first post was a photo showing an empty room with the now iconic yellow wallpaper, no natural lighting and a kind of inexplicable jutting half-wall. Shortly afterwards, another user (there are no usernames on 4chan, just identifying numbers) responded with 78 words of text that would essentially lay out the blueprint for a future $262m A24 movie sensation.
“If you’re not careful and you noclip out of reality in the wrong areas, you’ll end up in the Backrooms,” the post begins.
fullText:
The horror movie sensation of 2026 has its roots in gaming’s discovery of ‘noclip’ – and the hidden virtual realms that could be opened up inside games. Developers explain how everyone got lost in these liminal spaces

It starts on 4chan, in a May 2019 thread entitled “unsettling images”. The first post was a photo showing an empty room with the now iconic yellow wallpaper, no natural lighting and a kind of inexplicable jutting half-wall. Shortly afterwards, another user (there are no usernames on 4chan, just identifying numbers) responded with 78 words of text that would essentially lay out the blueprint for a future $262m A24 movie sensation.

“If you’re not careful and you noclip out of reality in the wrong areas, you’ll end up in the Backrooms,” the post begins. For the uninitiated, “noclip” refers to a game mode in which collision with solid objects is disabled, allowing players to move freely through walls and floors. Think of Chiwetel Ejiofor’s character in the film, finding a permeable wall in the basement of his furniture store and passing through to the world on the other side.

In games, noclip is intended for use by developers testing out their creations – but for decades now, players have been finding ways to access it themselves and reach hidden places they were never intended to see. It’s a phenomenon that Studio Chyr creative director William Chyr is intimately familiar with, both as a maker of games and as a player.

“Going behind the scenes, noclipping, and seeing the logic of the space, it’s like this Wizard of Oz moment of pulling open the curtain,” Chyr says. He remembers an early encounter with this in Batman: Arkham City: “There was this glitch that allowed you, if you kept spamming one of the grenades, to keep going higher and higher.” From there, the caped crusader could soar outside the level, into sections of Gotham that were only ever intended as a backdrop. “The streets had these cars that moved, but it was just a flat texture.”

Watching Backrooms, Chyr was also reminded of a similar bug in the notoriously janky Skyrim, where holding a wooden plate provided a quick way of noclipping out of the world. Looking at it from the outside in, players discovered that many of the game’s “tables” were in fact just bookcases embedded deep in the ground – just like the memorable Backrooms shot of a room in which the furniture is clipping through the floor. All these things that, in video games, the player is never meant to see.

The feel of Kane Parsons’ film is actually closer to these experiences than any of the many “official” Backrooms games that have popped up. The open-source nature of this mythos (as well as 4chan and Reddit, there are sprawling fan wikis cataloguing and expanding the lore) means that it’s possible to release your own game set in the Backrooms, using the name and iconography, in a way you couldn’t with another horror movie.

The most high-profile of these games, Escape the Backrooms, was first available in early-access form in August 2022, just months after Parsons’ first video. It offers a perfectly faithful recreation of the Backrooms aesthetic, from the yellow hallways to the yellow hazmat suits worn by agents of Async, the mysterious organisation only introduced towards the end of the film but a mainstay of the online incarnations. But all this is just wallpaper applied over the blueprint of a multiplayer survival horror game.

At its best, Backrooms taps into a sense of a place being “off”, in a way that’s unsettling but hard to pin down. It’s a delicate sensation, easily shattered (as it is in the film, I’d argue) by the presence of killer monsters. Even more so by the sight of another player in their gas mask and reindeer onesie, bunny-hopping through the hallways ahead.

Thankfully, there’s another stripe of Backrooms-inspired games offering nothing more than a self-guided tour through environments with a growing sense of weirdness and the constant suggestion of a threat lurking out of view.

Pools and Dreamcore both shine a spotlight on Poolrooms, an infinite swimming-baths dimension first glimpsed in one of Parsons’s videos and codified by the fandom as Level 37 of the Backrooms, with a similarly alien approach to architecture. In Dreamcore, it’s just one of a selection pack of realms to explore. You’ll also explore a “dead mall” and the looping corridors of a hotel: both abandoned and seemingly endless, like the spaces explored in the film, but with less of an obvious supernatural edge.

These malls and hotels are prime examples of a larger online taste for liminal spaces from which Backrooms is just one offshoot.

“These spaces always feel like they’re past their prime,” says Chyr. “It’s clear there was human activity here, at one point, but no longer.” His 2025 game Hotel Infinity is steeped in all these ideas, to the extent that at one point Hotel Liminal was considered as a title, Chyr says. “But I thought that was just too on the nose!”

Set in the lifeless corridors of a hotel seemingly designed by MC Escher, it’s a VR game that uses some clever spatial trickery to fold its endless halls into a 2x2m square of your living-room floor. One particular sequence late in Backrooms made me think of Chyr’s game – he confirms that he thought the same thing. “I was like, damn, I wish we’d done that!” he laughs.

Hotel Infinity is primarily focused on the impossible architecture of these places, something it shares with Exit 8 (also adapted into a film this year), a Japanese-made game that traps you in an infinitely looping section of a Tokyo metro station. The other side of the liminal coin is the sensation summoned by that original 4chan image: the eeriness of an empty place that no longer has any obvious function, or perhaps never did.

One game exploring this aspect is Interior Worlds, a “liminal photography” game in which you explore such spaces armed only with an SLR camera. The game’s developer, who goes by the moniker Sodaraptor, remembers first encountering the concept of liminal spaces “back in 2020, when the original Backrooms post on 4chan started going viral.”

It was an emotion they’d felt in such places but never previously had a name for. “A strange liminal discomfort”, Sodaraptor says, mixed with pangs of “anemoia”: nostalgia for an era that predates your own experience.

So it’s only fitting that the phenomenon’s virtual inspirations are now, in video game terms, as ancient as all those dead malls.

The aforementioned Arkham City and Skyrim both came out in 2011. The same year, Valve released Portal 2, the mind-bending first-person puzzler which Parsons has repeatedly cited as his biggest influence. The director even made a couple of Portal fan-videos; the last one was uploaded to his YouTube channel in 2021, just months before the first Backrooms clip.

It is probably inevitable that the aesthetics of these 15-year-old games would just now be beginning to seep through into the cinematic mainstream. Parsons was a young child when Portal 2 came out, and it’s only natural that he – and the generation of film-makers just now coming of age – would make things informed by the dark rooms they got lost in as kids.

A Minecraft Movie may already exist (unfortunately) but what will be much more interesting are the films and other artworks shaped by the experience of playing Minecraft at a formative age. Those dark caverns, the endless mines, the sounds of the zombies, the threat of the creepers – once those strange experiences have sunk into internet lore, who knows what will emerge and where it will take us.

title: I’ve been gaming for 40 years. Here are the best chairs in the UK for comfort, support and serious play
description:
Whether you’re on PC or a console, level up your setup with our gaming expert’s pick of the best chairs
• The best games of 2026 so far
Comfort is crucial to the gaming experience. It’s hard to focus on blasting aliens or taking Stoke to the Champions League final if your bum has gone to sleep because you’ve been sitting on an old chair for three hours. We’re spending more time playing games than ever before, so good posture matters. If you have set up a dedicated gaming space, then a rickety seat just won’t cut it.
From luxurious ergonomic thrones to cheap-and-cheerful bucket seats, the options available are bewildering.
fullText:
Whether you’re on PC or a console, level up your setup with our gaming expert’s pick of the best chairs

Comfort is crucial to the gaming experience. It’s hard to focus on blasting aliens or taking Stoke to the Champions League final if your bum has gone to sleep because you’ve been sitting on an old chair for three hours. We’re spending more time playing games than ever before, so good posture matters. If you have set up a dedicated gaming space, then a rickety seat just won’t cut it.

From luxurious ergonomic thrones to cheap-and-cheerful bucket seats, the options available are bewildering. So I set out on an epic quest: to find the most comfortable, durable and stylish gaming chairs. Here’s what I discovered.

Best gaming chair overall:

 Secretlab Titan Evo

Best budget gaming chair:

 ThunderX3 Solo 360

Best mid-range gaming chair:

 ThunderX3 Core

Best for combining gaming and working:

 Herman Miller x Logitech G Embody

Best for improving posture:

 Anthros the Chair

I have been playing video games for 40 years (gulp), and writing about them for my entire career as a journalist. I spend most of my waking hours sitting with a joypad in hand, and as a sufferer of lower back pain too (gee, I wonder why?), being comfortable while I’m “working” is vital. I’m also a veteran reviewer of gaming technology, including joypads, monitors, keyboards and headsets. In short, I know what people need from their games hardware.

I’m paid to sit and play video games all day (and often into the night), so that’s exactly what I did to test the chairs here. I started by noting how easy or challenging they were to assemble, how sturdy they felt and their level of adjustability. I also judged how cool they looked as part of my gaming setup.

I tested 10 gaming chairs over five days each, spending up to four hours a day sitting on them, playing a variety of games, from restful puzzlers to intense shooters and complex flight sims. I also sought the opinions of my sons, who are also keen gamers, and my wife – who isn’t at all interested in games, but who works from home, so was able to assess each model as an occasional office chair.

Once the testing process was finished, the chairs were donated to the video games accessibility charity, SpecialEffect, so that other people will get to enjoy them while blasting noobs in Fortnite.

Secretlab is a cool upmarket brand, beloved of many game streamers. Inside the box, the Titan Evo was packaged so neatly and stylishly, it felt as if I was unwrapping a giant iPhone. Although there are a lot of parts, I assembled it in less than 20 minutes, thanks to the poster-sized quick-start guide. My sample came in a sleek, matt-black leatherette finish, but there’s also a fabric version, plus a range of tasteful colours and designs to choose from. It comes in three sizes; I chose the XL because I like a LOT of space.

Why we love it
As a natural contrarian I wanted to dislike this much-hyped chair, but I couldn’t. The Titan is solid, beautiful and futuristic, looking like it’s been removed from the bridge of some extraordinarily luscious starship. The controls for the armrests and recline functions are well placed, with adjustments available to tweak the curvature and height of the lumbar support. The seat is capacious enough for lounging, and the leatherette is soft to the touch.

My wife found the seat too firm, and while I agreed initially, after a few days I realised it was helping me stay alert over long gaming sessions. Now, everything else feels like sitting on a marshmallow. (As an aside, I have also tried the new Evo NanoGen edition, which you may find offers a bit more give.)

The Titan Evo is neither cheap nor as ergonomically advanced as the Herman Miller or Anthros, yet it was the chair I looked forward to sitting in and really enjoyed using.

It’s a shame that … the warranty is only three years. You can extend it to five years by posting a photo of your chair on social media, but I dislike the idea of customer support being incentivised in this way.

Dimensions (XL version): 78 x 70 x 145cm (WDH)
Seat depth and height: 50cm, 46-55.5cm
Adjustments: lumbar support, armrests, recline, tilt lock
Brand’s sustainability claims: 90% of packaging is recycled paper content. Chair has modular design: if a component wears out over time, it can be replaced

A lot of so-called “ergonomic” gaming chairs at the sub-£200 price point are made with squeaky faux leather, plastic parts and sport brash designs – but not the Solo 360. Its slim build and muted grey and black colour options look sophisticated and are backed up with a solid steel construction. There are four variations – Racer, Mesh, Modern and the Loft Air Light version I tested – all in different materials.

Why we love it 
As well as being quick and easy to assemble, I was surprised by how comfortable the Solo 360 is, even over long periods – a view shared by my wife. The armrests are adjustable for both height and angle, and I welcomed the synchronous tilt, which reclines the back and the seat together for a laid-back feel, while your feet stay firmly on the ground. For less than £200, the ThunderX3 is a chair you can use for gaming, working and – possibly – sleeping.

It’s a shame that … the seat is rather low, and although the back is curved for lumbar support, the position wasn’t suitable for someone of my height (I’m 6ft 3in). However, this all makes it a good choice for shorter gamers.

Dimensions: 72-86 x 70 x 127-140cm (WDH) 
Seat depth and height: 48cm, 45-53cm
Adjustments: seat height, tilt, armrests, backrest resistance
Brand’s sustainability claims: armrests and wheels made of plastic contain 30% recycled materials. Metal products use approximately 70% recycled materials. Most components apart from leather, fabric and foam are recyclable. Spare parts available

Widely acclaimed by the gaming press, the ThunderX3 Core is a chunky, comfortable chair with a large winged back that envelops you. The chair offers several adjustability options, including the same synchronous tilt feature as the Solo, so the backrest and seat move together for ultimate comfort. I also appreciated the ability to slope the seat downwards, to really lean into the action yet take the pressure off the backs of my knees after hours of play.

Why we love it
The fabric version of the seat has the smoothest upholstery of all the chairs here – a really lovely soft feel. It also features a lumbar panel on the rear that moves with you as you lean from side to side, for excellent support while playing shooters and driving sims, for example. I didn’t like this feature as much for working, though.

It’s a shame that … although it’s easy to assemble, the heads of its hex screws are way too shallow and vulnerable to stripping. Also, the adjustment controls are awkwardly positioned and the armrests rattle a bit.

Dimensions: 70 x 70 x 129-139cm (WDH) 
Seat depth and height: 45-50cm, 46-56cm 
Adjustments: height, tilt, armrests
Brand’s sustainability claims: see ThunderX3 Solo 360 above

The Embody is Herman Miller’s premium gaming chair – and it shows. Whether you’re leaning into the screen or tilting back for a chilled session, its strong aluminium frame and high-end fabrics, including heat-dissipating composite particles, combine to keep you comfortable and cool. Available in a range of understated colours to suit more mature tastes, it arrives fully assembled – I was seated and playing Arc Raiders within 10 minutes of it being delivered.

Why we love it
The Embody is an impressively svelte chair. It has a narrow silhouette and a lower back than many of its competitors; there’s no headrest, nor does it offer some of the more intricate adjustments, such as 4D armrests or precise lumbar control. But it doesn’t need to – its clean, precise, ergonomic design gently encourages you to sit comfortably and correctly without you even realising.

There are levers allowing you to tilt fully, extend the seat depth or alter the back to fit your spine, but I didn’t have to spend ages getting everything right. The armrests are perfectly placed, the seat allows plenty of movement, and my spine felt cushioned, even when I spent all day in it – which made it great for work, too.

It’s a shame that … it’s expensive – but worth the money, if you’ll be using it for hours daily and it’s doubling as a home office chair. It comes with an impressive 12-year warranty, and when it does finally give up, the company claims it is up to 96% recyclable.

Dimensions: 74.9 x 38.1-45.7 x 106.7-114.3cm (WDH) 
Seat depth and height: 38.1-45.7cm; 43.2-55.9cm
Adjustments: seat height, seat depth, tilt and back fit, armrest height and width
Brand’s sustainability claims: corporate sustainability programme. Worn parts replaced free under warranty (outside that, UK customers are pointed to third-party suppliers). Made from 44% recycled materials. Chair is up to 96% recyclable at end of life

The Anthros is a serious piece of ergonomic equipment with intricately adjustable, well-placed controls for tilt, height and back support. Designed to stabilise your pelvis in order to alleviate back pain, its creators are as obsessed with posture as an overbearing Victorian governess – but in a good way. Indeed, the team used to design wheelchairs, so they know about ensuring long-term comfort.

Customers are even offered a complimentary video session with an expert in order to calibrate it properly. The chair frame comes in black or white, with a range of colours, textures and designs available for the rear of the backrest. It ships in two sections, so there’s little assembly.

Why we love it
As with the Herman Miller and Secretlab models, the Anthros offers a firm sit, with just the right amount of padding to keep glutes and upper thighs comfy. The back is made of two sections, one providing pelvis support, and the other gently cushioning your upper back – this part actually moves with you slightly as you lean left or right, which ensures you’re always in optimum contact with the chair. The decompress mode lets you tilt back and relax while still maintaining a healthy position.

After using it for a couple of weeks, I felt I was much better at sitting properly and experienced less of my usual pain when getting up. Whether I was bolt upright for hours writing articles, or wildly slamming about playing Call of Duty, it quite literally had my back.

It’s a shame that … it’s already pricey, but with US-only distribution pushing UK shipping costs to $307.71 (about £230) right now, it’s a significant investment. However, if you struggle with back pain, it’s excellent as a gaming and office chair.

Dimensions: 66 x 67 x 101.9-110.9cm (WDH)
Seat depth and height: 38.7-46.6cm, 48-59cm
Adjustments: tilt, seat height, upper and lower back
Brand’s sustainability claims: most parts are potentially recyclable (although it may be a struggle due to a lack of processing streams in the UK). Spare parts available. 12-year warranty

The Tempest is clearly aimed at a younger market, with sports car styling and fun LED panels that light up in a variety of colours. It was easy to assemble and feels pretty comfortable to sit in, with thick padding, a wide seat and rudimentary lumbar support. It’s a decent first gaming chair.

It didn’t make the final cut because … the build quality is basic, and there are no adjustment options apart from seat height. I’m not sure how it will hold up with regular use – although the one-year warranty covers replacement parts, and spares can be bought beyond that.

Dimensions: 69 x 67 x 114.5-122.5cm (WDH); seat depth and height: 60cm, 45-53cm; adjustments: height; brand’s sustainability claims: company is FIRA registered and audits factories to ensure best practices. Metal parts can be recycled. Parts can be exchanged for free under one-year warranty or bought outside that period at the manufacturer’s discretion

A bit more expensive than the Tempest, the Corsair comes in fabric and leatherette versions (I tested the fabric version) and has a wide seat designed to let you slob out a little as you play. It also comes with lumbar and neck pillows, and adjustable arms.

It didn’t make the final cut because … the racing car styling is cool, but the construction and materials lack the quality of more expensive models, and some parts were tricky to put together. It’s a decent entry-level gaming chair, but at this price, a dedicated office chair may be a better option for longer sessions and/or back pain sufferers.

Dimensions: 67 x 68 x 124-132cm (WDH); seat depth and height: 50cm, 45-55cm; adjustments: height, recline, armrests; brand’s sustainability claims: corporate sustainability programme. Comes with a two-year manufacturer’s guarantee

Best for: all-round performance

The Legend really does look like a sports car seat, with beautifully stitched faux leather fabric (vegan and sustainably made), a high-winged back, and sleek styling. There’s plenty of range to the tilt, and both the lumbar support and armrests are fully adjustable. I found it comfortable over long periods, so it can happily double as an office chair, plus it’s robust – and the company stocks spare parts, if needed.

It didn’t make the final cut because … I found the seat too shallow (I’m 6ft 3in) and the armrests uncomfortable, no matter how I adjusted them. There are slightly better options at this price point.

Dimensions: 52 x 73 x 132-142cm (WDH); seat depth and height: 48cm, 48-58cm; adjustments: tilt, armrests, lumbar support; brand’s sustainability claims: solvent- and phthalate-free materials and manufactured with low emissions. Metal parts recyclable. Chairs come with a two-year warranty covering parts

Best for: solid, sensible build quality

The Refine is an extremely well-built chair with a minimalist design that would suit the offices of some trendy Gothenburg architecture firm. Everything is easily adjustable, mostly via cool little tabs rather than the usual protruding levers, and the mesh fabric is comfortable and keeps you cool – although my younger son said it felt like sitting in a camping chair. Fractal also offers good after-care support, including spare parts.

It didn’t make the final cut because … the seat is a little shallow for taller users even at full extension, and I had to detach the headrest cushion as it was too invasive. Better as a quality office chair that you use occasionally for gaming, rather than the other way around.

Dimensions: 70 x 70 x 134-146.5cm (WDH); seat depth and height: 45-50.5cm, 49-61cm; adjustments: recline, height, armrests, lumbar support, headrest; brand’s sustainability claims: one more expensive Fractal Refine model uses Alcantara, a material with recycled elements. The company is moving to plastic‑free packaging. Metal sections can be recycled. Five-year warranty on mechanical parts and a three-year warranty on soft parts

If you only play console games for a few hours a week in front of a big TV in the living room, a nice slouchy armchair or even a beanbag is fine. However, if you play games at a desk with a monitor and want to feel comfortable, a decent chair is a good investment, especially for long gaming sessions, or if you also work at the desk from time to time.

It’s all about design purpose. An office chair is intended to support posture and productivity for several hours a day and will probably come with ergonomic features that allow you to fine-tune your sitting experience. A gaming chair is designed primarily for shorter-term comfort because, sadly, you’re unlikely to spend as much time playing games as you are working.

The design tends to focus on fun and immersion, which is why many look as if they’ve been pulled from a sports car or rollercoaster, featuring high-winged backs, headrests, lots of padding, and seats with raised edges. An office chair is usually conservative and unobtrusive; gaming chairs often sport a bolder look, with bright colours and extravagant design touches.

If you’re on a tight budget (£200 or less) and don’t care about flashy looks, an office chair is almost certainly a better choice, as they tend to be more sturdily built and ergonomically designed at this price.

For more, read our guide to the best office chairs

You need a chair that’s right for your size and gaming habits – for good posture, you should be able to plant your feet on the floor with your knees at a 90-degree angle and your upper legs parallel to the floor. If you’re a larger build or move a lot while playing, choose a chair with a wider, deeper seat. If you’re tall or experience back pain, go for an ergonomic model with good lumbar support.

Consider the way you play games. If you use a mouse and keyboard, then armrests are a good idea, but if you use a joypad and hold it close to your lap, they may get in the way of your elbows (unless they can be rotated, as chairs such as the Titan Evo, Anthros, Core and Refine allow). If you like to sit back with your feet up, make sure the chair has a deep tilt angle. If you’ll be working in your chair as well as gaming, consider a model with ergonomic features and more space to move about.

Think about how much time you will spend in the chair and how long you expect it to last. From £180, you can buy a comfortable, solidly built gaming chair that will suit most casual to intermediate gamers; from £350, models offer greater adjustability for posture and lumbar support, and are more likely to be built to last.

For more, read the best PS5 games to play in 2026 and the best of 2026 so far

As a veteran technology journalist, Keith Stuart has spent years testing gaming gadgets from headsets to keyboards to full PC builds, so he knows what gamers need. He also spends a disproportionate amount of time sitting down and so is doubly qualified to put gaming chairs through their paces

fullText:
Saturday, July 18th 2026

 Valve Reportedly Sells 12-15K Steam Machine Units Per Week

 by AleksandarK

 Yesterday, 16:38

 Discuss (72 Comments)

 When Valve listed its Steam Machine gaming console/PC back in late June, many doubted whether the console would sell due to its high price tag. However, it turns out that Valve's sales data have reportedly been good. Some investigative journalism led to an estimate that Valve is selling anywhere from 12,000 to 15,000 Steam Machine units per week. To reach that number, the Boiling Steam website used Steam's Global Top Sellers list, where Steam Machine is ranked as number two, right between Counter-Strike 2 and Palworld games. Based on data from multiple sources, the Boiling Steam estimation suggests that CS2 generates around $19-20 million in revenue, while third-place Palworld generates $7-9 million. This effectively places Steam Machine's revenue anywhere between $10-18 million per week. Considering that a weighted average distribution model shows most buyers, about 65%, are acquiring the base model priced at $1,049, the remaining 35% are purchasing the higher-tier $1,349 configuration.

The lower bound scenario suggests about 8,700 Steam Machine units sold per week, with the higher bound capped at about 15,600 units. A medium projection is about 12,000-15,000 units sold per week as of July 18, which is a healthy calculation. Since Valve keeps much of its information secretive, this estimation is one of the most concrete numbers we can get, all thanks to Boiling Steam's "napkin math." For the Steam Machine, which has been criticized for its high price tag, the sales numbers seem to be just okay, and the Steam community is buying these consoles in healthy numbers. If sales continue at this pace, there could be anywhere between 600,000 to 750,000 units sold in a year. Interestingly, we have to consider that this could be due to an elevated number of initial orders, and demand could drop in the coming weeks. It's not unusual to see sales volume dropping by 20-30% in the weeks following the initial hype, so we might get different data in the future. Boiling Steam plans on updating data estimations in the coming weeks as the market settles, so we will know with more certainty how sales are progressing over at Valve HQ.
